name: Formidable Care eRx
tagline: Electronic prescribing for clinicians: write a script, send it to the patient's pharmacy.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: An e-prescribing app is a thin UI bolted to a certified pipe you cannot build. Transmitting a prescription in the US means a Surescripts (or equivalent) connection, NCPDP SCRIPT conformance, a directory of every pharmacy's routing address, and for controlled substances DEA EPCS certification with third-party audit, identity proofing, and two-factor signing that meets 21 CFR 1311. None of that is code an agent writes in an afternoon; it is paperwork, audits, contracts, and a live network of pharmacies that already trust the sender. You can absolutely one-shot the form, the sig builder, the favorites list, and a nice PDF. What you cannot one-shot is anyone on the other end being legally allowed to fill it.
coreLoopDIY: A local prescription drafting tool: patient list, medication favorites, a sig builder, and a printable PDF Rx you sign by hand, with nothing transmitted anywhere.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine you control
A real DEA/NPI and prescribing authority if you intend to use printed scripts at all
Acceptance that printed and hand-signed is the only legal output here
Your own drug name list; no licensed clinical database included
whatYouLose: Actual transmission to pharmacies: no Surescripts connection, no NCPDP SCRIPT, no pharmacy directory
EPCS for controlled substances, which is a certified-audit problem, not a coding problem
Licensed drug data: RxNorm-mapped products, interaction and allergy checking, dosing rules, formulary and benefit checks
Refill requests, renewal responses, and prescription status coming back to you
Audit trails, HIPAA-grade hosting, BAAs, and the liability posture a clinician actually needs
Prior auth, medication history, and pharmacy stock signals
moatNotes: The certified transmission path is the product. The UI is decoration on top of a regulated pipe and a signed pharmacy network.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a prescription that cannot reach a pharmacy is a piece of paper, and paper is the thing everyone is trying to stop using. Clinicians pay for the certified route, the pharmacy directory, the controlled-substance flow that will survive a DEA audit, and someone else carrying the liability for a mis-transmitted dose. The vendor also absorbs the licensed clinical data bill and the interaction checking that keeps you out of court. A self-built version gets you a tidy PDF and none of the trust.
notes: The form is a weekend, the pipe is not. The moat is DEA and Surescripts certification plus every pharmacy in the country already agreeing to accept messages from them.
prompt:
Build a local-only prescription drafting tool for a single clinician. Nothing is transmitted; the only output is a printable PDF that a human signs by hand.

Stack, no alternatives: Node 20, TypeScript, Next.js App Router, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind, pdf-lib for PDF generation. Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost. No auth provider, no cloud, no telemetry, no external API calls at runtime.

Data model in SQLite:
- prescriber: name, credentials, NPI, DEA (optional), practice address, phone, fax
- patient: name, date of birth, address, phone, allergies (free text), notes
- medication: name, strength, form, route (this is a local list you seed and edit yourself, not licensed clinical data)
- favorite: medication reference plus a saved sig, quantity, refills, dispense-as-written flag
- prescription: patient, prescriber, one or more items, written date, status (draft, printed, voided), immutable copy of every printed version

Features in scope:
- Patient search and CRUD, with duplicate-name warning
- Sig builder: dose, route, frequency, duration, PRN reason, extra instructions, assembled into plain English plus a preview
- Favorites: save any composed item, one click to reuse
- Multi-item prescription drafts, printed as one PDF per item and as a combined summary sheet
- PDF layout: prescriber block, patient block with date of birth, date written, drug, sig, quantity in words and numerals, refills, signature line, and a footer reading "Print and sign. Not electronically transmitted."
- Print history: every PDF is written to ./out and logged; drafts are editable, printed records are not
- Local full-text search over patients and past prescriptions
- JSON export and import of the whole database

Explicitly out of scope, and say so in the README: any transmission to a pharmacy, Surescripts or NCPDP SCRIPT messaging, controlled-substance electronic signing, drug interaction or allergy checking, formulary or benefit lookup, refill request handling, RxNorm mapping, multi-user access.

Put a banner in the app shell: "Drafting aid only. No clinical decision support. No electronic transmission. Verify every field before signing."

Secrets, if any are ever added, go in .env with a committed .env.example. Seed the database with two fake patients and ten common medications so the app is usable on first run. Include a README with setup, the scope limits above, and a plain warning that this tool does not make anything legally transmissible.
